lessons.title: Anglicanism
lessons.subtitle: Complete document
content: The Anglican Communion is a global family of churches, present in more than 165 countries, walking together in mission and faith.

The Anglican Communion Office (ACO) is the official secretariat of the Anglican Communion, a worldwide network of Anglican churches in more than 165 countries. The ACO connects member churches, fosters global mission, encourages Christian unity, promotes ecumenism, and amplifies Anglican advocacy.

The ACO also supports and facilitates the 'Instruments of Communion': the Anglican Consultative Council, the Lambeth Conference, the Primates' Meeting, and the Archbishop of Canterbury.
What Anglicans believe
The Foundations of the Faith

The basis of Anglican faith is the fundamental Christian belief in the triune God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Anglicans believe that Jesus Christ, God the Son, lived, died, and rose again to restore humanity's broken relationship with God. This saving act, rooted in God's love, is the 'Good News' that Christians proclaim and the center of our shared faith.

Building on this foundation, Anglican identity is defined not only by what we believe, but by how we discern and articulate that faith.

content.text: The pillars of belief and practice

content: Our theological method

Anglicans discern the voice of God in the Holy Scriptures, as the ultimate rule and standard of faith. This guidance comes to us through the church's tradition, and we understand it using our capacity to think and reason.
Our shared faith

Anglicans affirm the ancient ecumenical Creeds as the sufficient statement of the Christian faith. The Apostles' and Nicene Creeds are a summary of the fundamental biblical truths that unite us with the Church, the one, holy, catholic, and apostolic.
Signs of God's grace

A sacrament is an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace. Anglicans celebrate the two great sacraments of the Gospel, Baptism and the Eucharist, as effective channels of God's grace and indispensable to our life of faith.
Our framework for unity

This foundational statement identifies the four essential elements of our faith and order: the Scriptures, the Creeds, the Sacraments, and the Historic Episcopate. It serves both as a touchstone for Anglican identity and as a basis for Christian unity.
A lived faith
Anglican beliefs are not static principles, but are understood as a living faith. This faith is actively expressed through three key dimensions:
History of Anglicanism

The Anglican Communion is a worldwide family of churches. It is the third-largest Christian communion in the world, after the Roman Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox churches. The communion is composed of 42 independent national or regional churches, including the Church of England, the Episcopal Church (USA), the Anglican Church of Kenya, the Anglican Church of Southern Africa, and many others. Each church is autonomous—that is, it governs itself—but united by a shared history, liturgy, and episcopal structure.

The history of Anglicanism is not the story of a single founder or of a rigid confession of faith. It is the story of the 'Anglican Way', a particular and historical expression of the Christian faith that seeks to be a faithful continuation of the 'One, Holy, Catholic, and Apostolic Church of Jesus Christ'. This 'Way', which forms a fundamental part of what Anglicans believe, was forged in the unique crucible of the English Reformation, establishing a distinctive approach to faith, worship, and mission that now connects a global family of churches.

The Anglican Communion emerged from the Church of England. This has its roots in the ancient Celtic churches of Ireland and Britain and in the mission of St Augustine of Canterbury and his fellow monks from Rome, a mission that landed in Kent in AD 597. He and later Archbishops of Canterbury, especially Theodore, played a fundamental role in establishing Christianity in England. For nearly a thousand years, the church in England was an integral part of the Western Church in communion with Rome.

When Augustine was sent to Kent in AD 597 by Pope Gregory the Great, he established his see and the first cathedral. In the 1170s, the murder of Archbishop Thomas Becket transformed the cathedral into a major European place of pilgrimage. As Anglicanism spread throughout the world over the centuries, Canterbury Cathedral came to be seen by many Anglicans as a place of historical and symbolic importance.

content.text: The Church of England breaks with Rome

content:
The English Reformation, begun by Henry VIII in the 1530s, cut the Church in England's ties with Rome, establishing the monarch as Supreme Governor of the Church of England. It also tilted England toward Protestantism, bringing lasting religious, political, and cultural changes.

After a period of religious volatility, Queen Elizabeth I's Religious Settlement (c. 1559) established a unified national church. It followed a path known as the via media, or "middle way", one of considering different viewpoints and finding pastoral and practical ways forward for the church and the nation. It created a church that was both 'catholic and reformed', one that maintained the ancient catholic order of bishops, priests, and deacons, while embracing the Protestant Reformation's emphasis on the supreme authority of Scripture. This identity received its intellectual foundation through the theologian Richard Hooker, who defended a balanced approach to authority.

content.text: The three pillars: Scripture, Tradition, and Reason

content: From Hooker's work develops the classic Anglican theological method, often described as a 'three-legged stool'. It is not a static formula, but a dynamic and interactive method for discerning truth.
Scripture: The Holy Scriptures are the supreme standard of faith, containing all that is necessary for salvation.
Tradition: The wisdom of the Church handed down through the centuries—including the Creeds and the teachings of the early Church—is a vital resource that helps us interpret the Scriptures faithfully.
Reason: The God-given faculty for critical thought enables us to interpret the Scriptures, learn from Tradition, and apply our faith to the challenges of our contemporary context.

This balanced method allows Anglicanism to be a reflective, non-fundamentalist, and context-sensitive faith, providing the 'software' that enables a diverse global Communion to navigate complex questions over time, though not always without disagreement and debate.

content.text: Anglicanism and the Book of Common Prayer

content:
Archbishop Thomas Cranmer was a major theological architect of the English Reformation era. He crafted the Book of Common Prayer (1549, 1552), a revolutionary liturgy in the English language. This reformed theology—such as the authority of Scripture and justification by faith—permeated people's hearts and minds through their weekly worship. This established a defining Anglican characteristic: finding unity through common prayer, or lex orandi, lex credendi (the law of prayer is the law of belief).

The Book of Common Prayer became a significant book for many Anglicans around the world. It has evolved into a global family of prayer books used in more than 50 countries and 150 languages.

content.text: The Anglican Communion: A global network of churches

content:
Historically, sharing the faith and missionary activity have always been a distinctive feature of Christianity. In the "Great Commission" (Matthew 28:18–20), Jesus instructed his followers to make disciples of all nations, and this remains a central call for the global Church.

Like many Christian churches, Anglicanism became a worldwide communion through several interconnected processes. During the sixteenth and twentieth centuries, the Church's missionary work became intertwined with European exploration and the colonial expansionism of the era.

Missionary efforts Anglican missionary societies established churches, schools, and hospitals in Africa, Asia, the Pacific, and the Americas. These efforts were complex: although missionaries often operated within colonial power structures, many also advocated for indigenous peoples and translated the scriptures into local languages, inadvertently providing tools for both cultural preservation and transformation.

Indigenous leadership and adaptation Indigenous Christians often adapted Anglican traditions to their own cultural contexts, creating distinctly local expressions of faith. African, Asian, and Pacific Island Christians developed their own theological voices and eventually assumed leadership roles.

A complex legacy Although Anglicanism provided communal and spiritual meaning to millions, its expansion often came at a tremendous cost to indigenous cultures and was implicated in colonial oppression. An honest appraisal of this history requires acknowledgment.

The mid-twentieth century brought a fundamental shift. The former colonial churches became autonomous provinces within the Anglican Communion, led by local bishops and clergy.

A crucial development in Anglican history was the evolution from missionary dioceses, controlled by the Church of England, to fully autonomous (self-governing) churches. This was not only a political necessity, but a theological fulfillment of Anglicanism's own principles of shared governance and local leadership through bishops.

The Episcopal Church in the United States, formed after the American Revolution, set the first precedent. This was followed by churches around the world, especially in the mid-twentieth century, when they achieved political independence and began to adapt their worship and life to their own cultural contexts.

The result of this history is the Anglican Communion of the twenty-first century: a global family with an estimated 90 million members in more than 165 countries. It connects 42 autonomous and interdependent national and regional churches, known as provinces.

A defining characteristic of the modern Communion is the dramatic demographic shift of its center of gravity. The vast majority of active Anglicans now live in the Global South, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, a reality that shapes the Communion's priorities and conversations.

content.text: The instruments of the Anglican Communion

content:
What holds this diverse global family of churches together? The Anglican Communion has no central government or single figure with binding legal authority.

Instead, unity is sought through a set of relational and consultative bodies known as the Instruments of Communion. Their purpose is to bring together the leaders and people of the Communion for prayer, counsel, and fellowship, fostering the 'bonds of affection' that are the glue of our global family.
The Archbishop of Canterbury: A 'focus of unity' for the Communion, who convenes its members in different ways.
The Lambeth Conference: A gathering of bishops from across the Communion for prayer, study, and shared discernment, traditionally held every ten years.
The Anglican Consultative Council (ACC): The representative body of the Communion, uniquely including bishops, clergy, and laity in its membership.
The Primates' Meeting: A gathering of the senior archbishops and presiding bishops from each province for prayer and consultation.

content.text: Serving the world: our ecumenical and missionary vocation

content: The Anglican Way is not an end in itself. From its foundations, Anglicanism has understood itself as part of the universal Church, with a mission that goes beyond its own boundaries.

Anglicans are deeply committed to building ecumenical relationships and working for the visible unity of the Church. Our unique identity as 'catholic and reformed' enables Anglicanism to act as a 'bridge church', finding common ground with the Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches, as well as with Protestant traditions.

The Anglican Communion actively participates in formal dialogues with most of the world's major Christian families. We are in 'full communion' with bodies such as the Old Catholic Churches of the Union of Utrecht and the Mar Thoma Syrian Church of Malabar, which allows us to share a common eucharistic life.

content.text: Anglicans and mission in the world

content: The ultimate purpose of the Church is to participate in the mission of God (missio Dei). Missio Dei is Latin and means 'the Mission of God'. It refers to the belief that God is the primary agent of mission, actively working to reconcile, restore, and redeem all creation through Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit. Rather than the church having a mission, the church actively participates in God's mission. In the Anglican tradition, this idea is expressed through the Five Marks of Mission, which are widely adopted throughout the Communion as a framework for our work.
Tell: To proclaim the Good News of the Kingdom.
Teach: To teach, baptize, and nurture new believers.
Tend: To respond to human need by loving service.
Transform: To seek to transform unjust structures of society, to challenge violence of every kind, and to pursue peace and reconciliation.
Treasure: To strive to safeguard the integrity of creation and sustain and renew the life of the earth.
Five Marks of Mission
The five marks of mission

content.text:
The Five Marks of Mission are a foundational framework that defines the Anglican Communion's common commitment to God's holistic and integral mission. They offer a comprehensive vision of how the Church participates in God's redemptive work in the world.

Although deeply theological, the Marks are also a practical tool. They offer parishes and dioceses around the world a memorable 'checklist' for missionary activities. This ensures that as a community focuses on one area of mission, no other essential component—from evangelism to care for creation—is inadvertently neglected.

content: A foundational mandate: The mission of the Church is the mission of Christ

content.text:
The entire framework of the Five Marks of Mission rests on a single fundamental principle: 'The mission of the Church is the mission of Christ'.

This statement is the interpretive key to the framework. It establishes that the Church does not invent its own mission; rather, it is called to participate in the mission of God revealed in the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.

Within this structure, the First Mark—proclaiming the 'Good News of the Kingdom'—functions as the primary lens through which the other four are understood.

content: The other marks are the necessary expressions of what the 'Good News of the Kingdom' is in practice.
A memorable framework for action

content.text:
To facilitate their practical application, many churches and dioceses have adopted a simple mnemonic as a memorable way to apply this holistic framework:

Tell, Teach, Tend, Transform, and Treasure.

This helps to easily remember the five marks and put them into practice, with each word corresponding to one of the official statements:

content:
A living framework:
The evolution of the marks

content.text: The Five Marks of Mission are a dynamic framework that has evolved to meet contemporary challenges.

content: The marks are not a final statement, but a guide that the Communion regularly reviews.
1984: The Anglican Consultative Council (ACC-6) was the first to develop the four marks, balancing evangelism and social action.
1990: The Anglican Consultative Council at 'ACC-8' adds the Fifth Mark in response to a growing understanding of the global ecological crisis and the biblical call to care for creation.
2012: The Anglican Consultative Council at 'ACC-15' refines the wording of the Fourth Mark to include more explicitly the pursuit of peace and reconciliation.
Many Anglican churches have adopted the Five Marks of Mission in their settings around the world.

TELL
Proclaim the Good News of the Kingdom

This first mark is the source of all missionary activity. Identified with personal evangelism at the Anglican Consultative Council in 1984, it is the non-negotiable verbal witness of the Christian faith. The proclamation is of the "Kingdom of God", God's sovereign, redeeming, and restoring rule over all life. This broad concept announces that in Jesus Christ, God acts to heal, reconcile, and make all things new, providing the theological foundation for the other four marks.

content.text:
TEACH
Teach, baptize, and nurture new believers

content: Flowing directly from proclamation, this second mark addresses the essential work of discipleship. It affirms that the Church's responsibility does not end at conversion, but requires intentional processes of teaching the faith, incorporating people into the community through baptism, and providing ongoing spiritual support. This ensures the long-term sustainability and spiritual depth of the Church, forming mature disciples who, in turn, can participate in God's mission.

content.text:
TEND
Respond to human need by loving service

content: The third mark is rooted in Jesus' example of compassionate action, which embodies the presence of the Kingdom of God through care for the sick, poor, and vulnerable, reflects the Great Commandment to love God and neighbor, and demonstrates that service is central to the faith, transforming lives and society through practical love and justice.

content.text:
TRANSFORM
Transform the unjust structures of society, challenge violence of every kind, and pursue peace and reconciliation

content: The fourth mark represents the prophetic dimension of mission. It demonstrates a sophisticated understanding that sin is not only personal but also systemic. It calls the Church to go beyond individual acts of charity (Mark 3) to address the root causes of suffering: the "unjust structures" that perpetuate poverty, oppression, and conflict. The call to challenge violence and pursue peace insists that holistic mission must engage the political, economic, and social systems that shape human life.

content.text:
TREASURE
Strive to safeguard the integrity of creation and sustain and renew the life of the earth

content: The fifth mark articulates the ecological dimension of mission, expanding the circle of responsibility to its fullest extent. Formally added in 1990, this mark reflects a mature theological understanding that God's redemptive plan is cosmic in scope. It calls human beings to their divinely assigned role as guardians of the earth, presenting environmental care not as a secular agenda, but as an integral component of fidelity to God the Creator.
The role of Scripture, Tradition, and Reason

content.text: The role of Scripture, Tradition, and Reason

content:
A fundamental hallmark of Anglican identity is not only what Anglicans believe, but how we arrive at and articulate those beliefs.

The Anglican theological method is best understood as a dynamic and integrated process. Anglicans seek to discern the voice of the living God in the Holy Scriptures, mediated by tradition and reason. This hermeneutic anchors the faith, providing a common grammar for theological discourse across the diverse global Anglican Communion.

Although often simplified as a 'three-legged stool', this analogy can be misleading if it implies three equal or competing sources of authority. A more accurate model is an interpretive ecosystem with a clear hierarchy: the Scriptures are the foundational source, understood through the prism of Tradition and engaged by God-given reason.

content.text: Scripture: The supreme standard of faith

content:
The Anglican Communion is anchored in a deep commitment to the authority of the Holy Scriptures. Anglicans affirm the Bible as the ultimate rule and standard of faith, containing all that is necessary for salvation.
Anglicans approach the Bible with a clear Christ-centered quality. Anglicans believe that the first and eternal Word of God is Jesus Christ, to whom all Scripture bears witness. He is the hermeneutical key, the one through whom the Holy Spirit reveals to us the meaning of the Scriptures.

This commitment is not merely a formal doctrine; it is woven into the fabric of Anglican common life. The Scriptures are central to worship, prayed and sung through liturgy and hymnody, and read in community through the Daily Office and the lectionaries.

content.text: Tradition: The living context for interpretation

content:
The Scriptures are never read in a vacuum. They are mediated by tradition, which Anglicans understand not as a parallel authority, but as the 'dynamic and continuous stream' of the Church's faith, worship, and order, flowing from the Apostles to the present day.

This living stream includes two interconnected currents:

The Great Tradition: This is the consensual faith of the early and undivided Church, expressed in the ecumenical Creeds. The Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed function as the regula fidei, or 'rule of faith'

The Anglican heritage: This is the particular stream of Anglicanism's tradition that gives Anglicans a distinctive character. It includes historic formularies and polity, especially the Book of Common Prayer, the Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion, and our commitment to the Historic Episcopate.

content.text: Reason: The God-given gift for discernment

content:
Reason is the third component of Anglican hermeneutics, understood as a critical faculty granted by God that operates in the service of faith, not in opposition to it. Anglicans believe that faith and intellect are partners in the pursuit of truth.

Reason fulfills a dual function:
Critical Engagement: It enables a 'grateful and critical sense of the past', allowing Anglicans to analyze the Scriptures and Tradition in their original contexts.

Constructive engagement: It facilitates a vigorous engagement with the present, helping Anglicans to apply the eternal truths of the Gospel to new situations and to new expressions of a faith informed by the scriptures.

content.text: The method in practice: a living framework

content:
This theological method is not an abstract theory; it is put into operation in the corporate life of the Communion through our Instruments of Communion:

1. The Lambeth Conference
2. The Anglican Consultative Council
3. The Primates' Meeting 4. The Archbishop of Canterbury

The Inter-Anglican Standing Commission on Unity, Faith and Order (IASCUFO) is a clear example of this method in action. As the Communion's principal body for theological reflection, IASCUFO applies disciplined and scholarly reason to the scriptures and tradition to address the Communion's most complex challenges. Its work on the biblical concept of koinonia (communion), for example, laid the theological foundations necessary for The Nairobi-Cairo Proposals, applying this framework to the real challenge of navigating disagreement and renewing our structures for a postcolonial era.
The Creeds: Our Statement of Faith

content.text: The Creeds: Our Statement of Faith

content: The ancient Creeds are the living voice of the Church, connecting Anglicans in our diverse and global Communion with the 'One, Holy, Catholic, and Apostolic Church' of all times and places.

content.text: Anglican faith is a shared faith

content:
The faith of Anglicanism is not a new invention. It is the same faith held by the Apostles and the undivided Church of the first centuries. The Creeds are the foundational and ecumenical statements of this universal, or 'catholic', faith.

The Anglican Communion holds the three historic Creeds as foundational statements of the Christian faith:
The Apostles' Creed
The Nicene Creed
The Athanasian Creed

Anglicans affirm these Creeds because their fundamental principles can be historically proved by Holy Scripture. They are not an alternative to the Bible, but a summary of the fundamental truths of the Scriptures, forming a tower with solid foundations for Christian doctrine.

content.text: Belief Shaped by Prayer (Lex Orandi, Lex Credendi)

content:
A fundamental Anglican principle is Lex orandi, lex credendi – 'the law of praying is the law of believing'. This means that doctrine is not just an abstract list of rules, but a lived reality, 'found and internalized through collective worship.

The classic Book of Common Prayer (BCP) and the service books that have followed it are the primary expression of this principle. They weave the Creeds directly into the living fabric of Anglican worship, shaping the faith every time we pray together as a community.
Anglican liturgy uses the three historic Creeds in distinct contexts, each with a specific purpose in the life of the Church.
What it is: The Apostles' Creed is the ancient baptismal creed of the Church, used historically to summarize the central narrative of the Christian faith for those preparing for Baptism
How it is used: It is the principal creed used in Baptism services and in the daily offices of Morning and Evening Prayer

content.text: The text of the Apostles' Creed:

content:
I believe in God, the Father almighty,
creator of heaven and earth.
I believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord,
who was conceived by the Holy Spirit,
born of the Virgin Mary,
suffered under Pontius Pilate,
was crucified, died, and was buried;
he descended to the dead.
On the third day he rose again;
he ascended into heaven,
he is seated at the right hand of the Father,
and he will come to judge the living and the dead.
I believe in the Holy Spirit,
the holy catholic Church,
the communion of saints,
the forgiveness of sins,
the resurrection of the body,
and the life everlasting.
Amen.
What it is: The Nicene Creed was formulated at the great Councils of the Church of Nicaea (AD 325) and Constantinople (AD 381).
Purpose: It was written to articulate the Church's definitive and orthodox understanding of the full divinity of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit in response to early theological debates.

How it is used: It is the principal creed recited by the congregation during Holy Communion (Eucharist). This act unites the whole community in a common profession of faith before approaching the Lord's Table.

content.text: The text of the Nicene Creed:

content:
We believe in one God,
the Father, the Almighty,
maker of heaven and earth,
of all that is,
seen and unseen.
We believe in one Lord, Jesus Christ,
the only Son of God,
eternally begotten of the Father,
God from God, Light from Light,
true God from true God,
begotten, not made,
of one Being with the Father;
through him all things were made.
For us and for our salvation he came down from heaven,
was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary
and was made man.
For our sake he was crucified under Pontius Pilate;
he suffered death and was buried.
On the third day he rose again
in accordance with the Scriptures;
he ascended into heaven
and is seated at the right hand of the Father.
He will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead,
and his kingdom will have no end.
We believe in the Holy Spirit,
the Lord, the giver of life,
who proceeds from the Father and the Son,
who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified,
who has spoken through the prophets.
We believe in one holy catholic and apostolic Church.
We acknowledge one baptism for the forgiveness of sins.
We look for the resurrection of the dead,
and the life of the world to come.
Amen.
What it is: The Athanasian Creed is a detailed and classic exposition of the orthodox doctrines of the Trinity (the nature of God) and the Incarnation (the person of Jesus Christ).

How it is used: Although it is an official formulary, this creed is used much less in public worship today. It remains highly valued for its precise theological clarity on these 'key Christian doctrines'.

The Creeds are a 'non-negotiable core' of Anglicanism. They are also fundamental to ecumenical efforts, since the Creeds are shared by Roman Catholics, the Eastern Orthodox, and many Protestant churches. They serve as a powerful bridge for dialogue and a witness to the shared faith.

This foundational Anglican document, adopted in 1888, describes four essential elements for a reunited Christian Church.

The second of these four points is: the Apostles' Creed, as the baptismal symbol; and the Nicene Creed, as the sufficient statement of the Christian faith.

This demonstrates the central role the Creeds play in Anglican identity and our mission to seek the visible unity of all Christians.
The Sacraments: Signs of God's Grace

content.text: The Sacraments: Signs of God's Grace

content:
For Anglicans, a sacrament is 'an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace'. This means that they are physical and tangible actions, instituted by Christ, that serve as effective channels for divine grace and God's work in our lives.

They are not just memorials or empty symbols; They are efficacious, that is, they actually effect what they signify. This understanding is at the heart of Anglican worship, where our relationship with God is nourished through the inseparable union of 'word and sacrament': the reading of the Scriptures and the celebration of these sacred rites.

This connection between worship and belief is a fundamental part of Anglican identity, captured in the ancient Christian principle lex orandi, lex credendi (the law of praying is the law of believing). Our doctrine is expressed and preserved in our collective worship.

As a fundamental part of what Anglicans believe, the sacraments are indispensable to our life of faith.

content.text: The Two Great Sacraments of the Gospel

content:
The Anglican Communion gives special status to two sacraments: Baptism and the Eucharist (also known as Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper).

They are often called 'dominical sacraments' because they were ordained directly by Christ in the Gospels. They are understood as 'generally necessary for salvation' for all Christians, forming the basis of Christian life and mission.

Baptism is the fundamental sacrament of initiation through which a person becomes a member of the Church of God, the Body of Christ. It is much more than a symbolic washing; it is a profound participation in the saving work of Jesus.
Participation in Christ: Through the waters of baptism, the believer is united with Christ in his death, burial, and resurrection
Gift of the Spirit: In baptism, God grants the gift and promise of the Holy Spirit, sealing the believer as Christ's own forever
A bond of unity: Our common baptism is the 'basic bond of unity' that Anglicans share with all Christians

content.text: The Eucharist (Holy Communion): Sustenance and Communion

content: If Baptism is the sacrament of our initiation, the Eucharist is the Church's shared 'family meal' that continually sustains and nourishes us.
Anamnesis (Sacramental Memorial): The Eucharist is a sacramental memorial where, by the power of the Holy Spirit, Christ's once-and-for-all sacrifice on the cross is 'made present and effective'
The real presence: Anglicans affirm that Christ is truly present in the Eucharist. The bread and wine 'become' the body and blood of Christ in a sacramental sense to transform people
Beyond the two great sacraments, the Anglican tradition celebrates five other sacramental rites. These are true and valuable means of communicating God's grace in specific moments and vocations.
Confirmation: A mature and public affirmation of the baptismal vows, strengthened by the Holy Spirit for a life of discipleship
Ordination (Holy Orders): Also known as Holy Orders; the rite in which God grants grace and authority to bishops, priests, and deacons
Marriage (Holy Matrimony): A faithful, lifelong covenant between two people, serving as a sign of Christ's love for his Church
Reconciliation of a Penitent (Confession): Often called Confession; a rite in which a person receives the assurance of forgiveness and the grace of absolution
Anointing of the Sick (Healing): Commending the sick to God's care, seeking spiritual and physical healing and the grace to persevere in faith

Our shared understanding of the sacraments, especially Baptism and the Eucharist, is a vital part of our dialogue with other Christian traditions. Reaching a 'substantial agreement' on the Eucharist is an important and joyful step toward the visible unity of all Christians that Christ desires for his Church.
Liturgy and Worship

Worship deeply shapes Anglican spiritual identity. The ancient Christian principle of Lex orandi, lex credendi – meaning "the law of praying is the law of believing" – illustrates the deep relationship between worship and belief. For Anglicans, liturgical celebrations arise directly from the mystery of salvation in Jesus Christ and form part of the very means by which the faithful enter into that mystery.

Liturgy does not function simply as a static set of historical rubrics, but as a dynamic pedagogical framework designed to shape the spiritual life, theological understanding, and missional identity of the faithful. While the autonomous provinces within the Anglican Communion possess their own localized Books of Common Prayer, adapted to specific cultural and linguistic contexts, the global church continually strives to pray with a single, unified voice.
The coordination of these complex liturgical practices across disparate geographic and cultural contexts is facilitated primarily through the International Anglican Liturgical Consultation (IALC).

Since the Anglican Communion operates intrinsically as a voluntary communion of autonomous national and regional churches, the coordination of sensitive liturgical matters is facilitated horizontally. This "Network Approach" relies on rigorous consensus-building, bringing together theological experts, practicing liturgists, and officially designated provincial representatives to synthesize localized traditions into universally acceptable formats.
The ongoing work of the IALC and of global liturgists focuses on several key themes to enrich the daily worship life of the international Anglican community:
The ongoing work of the IALC and of global liturgists focuses on several key themes to enrich the daily worship life of the international Anglican community:

Praying with one voice: A commitment to eucharistic renewal and sacramental standardization. This work focuses on creating harmonized worship practices and common liturgical texts so that Anglicans from disparate global regions can gather and worship without prioritizing one provincial tradition over another.

Equipping the Saints: A deep theological belief that the architecture, vocabulary, and physical actions of collective worship actively shape Christian identity. This democratization of worship emphasizes comprehensive liturgical formation for all baptized members, rejecting the idea that a deep liturgical understanding is the exclusive domain of the ordained clergy.

Shared time: A synchronized approach to how the global church relates to the sacred scriptures and navigates the annual rhythms of the traditional church calendar, effectively connecting the daily, weekly, and seasonal biblical reflections of the whole Communion.

Contextualization of pastoral rites: Ongoing theological review and renewal of foundational rites, such as marriage, providing a grounded framework for local clergy to navigate the intersection between global Anglican theology and localized cultural rites of passage.
The Anglican Communion produces a rich and complex synthesis of standardized rites, pastoral guidelines, and formative frameworks.

Praying with one voice: A common and officially endorsed eucharistic prayer, designed specifically for international and transprovincial use, that allows diverse assemblies to participate together in the church's central sacrament.
The Berkeley Statement: 'Equipping the Saints': A foundational document that frames comprehensive liturgical education as a vital mechanism for the spiritual empowerment of the wider church body.
Rationale for the Lectionary: The underlying theological logic and explanatory notes for the specific cycle of biblical reading used universally within the Anglican Cycle of Prayer.
The Chicago-Lambeth Quadrilateral

The Chicago-Lambeth Quadrilateral is a foundational statement that identifies the four essential elements of faith and order that Anglicans consider necessary for Christian unity. It serves both as an essential touchstone for Anglican identity and as a definitive basis for the Communion's ecumenical dialogues with other Christian churches.
The Four Points
The Quadrilateral defines the Communion's commitment to four key elements:
The Holy Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, as "containing all things necessary to salvation", and as being the rule and ultimate standard of faith.
The Apostles' Creed, as the baptismal symbol; and The Nicene Creed, as the sufficient statement of the Christian faith.
The two sacraments ordained by Christ himself—Baptism and the Lord's Supper—ministered with unfailing use of Christ's words of Institution and of the elements ordained by Him.
The Historic Episcopate, locally adapted in the methods of its administration to the varying needs of the nations and peoples called of God into the Unity of His Church.
A framework for ecumenical dialogue

The Quadrilateral was first formulated in Chicago, USA, in 1886 and was formally adopted by the Lambeth Conference of Anglican bishops in 1888.

Its original purpose was to provide a clear and stable framework for pursuing "Home Reunion": the healing of divisions among Christian churches. It remains the basis on which the Anglican Communion engages in ecumenical dialogues, offering these four points as an essential foundation for discussions on achieving visible Christian unity.
A touchstone for Anglican identity

Although its origins are ecumenical, the Quadrilateral also functions as an "essential touchstone for Anglican identity". For the autonomous member churches of the Anglican Communion, it articulates a shared and common commitment to these foundational principles of Scripture, faith, sacrament, and structure.
Explore Our Foundations
The Quadrilateral is a key part of the shared heritage that informs The Instruments of Communion and their work of fostering unity and mission throughout the world.
What are the instruments of communion?
The instruments of communion

content.text: The 'Instruments of Communion' exist to promote unity and collaboration in the Anglican Communion. The ACO serves each of the instruments and organizes relevant meetings. The instruments are the Anglican Consultative Council, the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Primates' Meeting, and the Lambeth Conference.

content: The Anglican Consultative Council

The Anglican Consultative Council (ACC) is one of the four Instruments of Communion that serve and strengthen the global Anglican Communion. It holds a unique position as the most representative body of the Communion, distinguished by the inclusion of bishops, clergy, and laity from all member provinces.

Read the ACC Constitution
Click here to access the ACC-19 event webpage
The next ACC plenary meeting will be hosted by the Church of Ireland in Belfast from 27 June to 5 July 2026.

content.text: A unique role in the communion

content:
The ACC was formed in response to a resolution of the 1968 Lambeth Conference that recognized the need for a body that included clergy and laity in the international life of the Communion.

It is the only Instrument of Communion that brings together bishops, clergy, and laity, ensuring a synodical principle at the international level. The Council is explicitly a consultative body, not an international synod, and has no legal or legislative power over the autonomous provinces. Its authority is moral and relational, providing a crucial forum for the "whole church" in its discernment and shared life.

content.text: The purpose and mandate of the ACC

content: The Anglican Consultative Council (ACC) enables the autonomous churches of the Communion to work together more effectively. Its main constitutional functions are:
To advise on the organization and structures of the communion.
To seek to develop common policies on the worldwide mission of the Church, including ecumenical matters.
To facilitate the cooperative work of the member churches and strengthen the bonds of friendship that unite them.
The ACC often serves as an incubator for foundational theological and missiological frameworks at the Communion level.
The Five Marks of Mission: This framework, which defines the Church's holistic mission, was first articulated in a report to the ACC-6 meeting in Badagry, Nigeria, in 1984.

Inclusion and representation: The ACC has pioneered greater inclusion in the Communion's structures. It was the first Instrument to formally include youth delegates as full voting members, a process that began at the ACC-17 meeting in Hong Kong.
The composition of the ACC is designed to ensure broad and balanced representation from across the Communion.

Membership: The Council is composed of approximately 100 members. Each of the Communion's provinces sends two or three representatives (bishops, clergy, and laity). Members typically serve for three consecutive meetings to foster continuity and institutional memory.
Leadership: The Council's work is guided by a formal leadership structure:
President: The Archbishop of Canterbury (ex officio).
Chair: Canon Maggie Swinson.
Vice-Chair: Archbishop Hosam Naoum.
Secretariat: The Anglican Communion Office (ACO), led by the Secretary General, facilitates and supports the Council's meetings and work.

content.text:
Plenary meetings:
The Anglican Consultative Council in action

content:
The principal expression of the ACC's work is its plenary meeting, which convenes approximately every three years and is hosted by a different member province.

Each meeting includes communal Bible study, updates from member churches and Anglican networks, and the adoption of resolutions that help coordinate the Communion's work in mission and ministry.

The first meeting (ACC-1) was held in Limuru, Kenya, in 1971. The most recent was ACC-18 in Accra, Ghana (2023). The next, ACC-19, will be hosted by the Church of Ireland in Belfast from 27 June to 5 July 2026.

content.text: Reporting to ACC-19 on the Nairobi-Cairo Proposals

content: At its 2023 meeting, the ACC passed a resolution commissioning a "renewed exploration of 'structure and decision-making'" to help address differences within the Communion.
This task was taken up by the Inter-Anglican Standing Commission on Unity, Faith and Order (IASCUFO).

IASCUFO shared The Nairobi-Cairo Proposals in Advent. A supplementary article was shared in Lent 2026. The proposals are presented as an "offer" to the whole Communion and the "beginning of a new conversation" about how to navigate differences and maintain unity.
Formal consideration of these proposals will be one of the key agenda items for the upcoming ACC-19 meeting in Belfast.
The Archbishop of Canterbury
The Archbishop of Canterbury

content.text:
The Archbishop of Canterbury is one of the four Instruments of Communion that together seek to foster unity in the global Anglican family. The Archbishop holds a unique position within the Communion, as the first bishop of the first historic see, founded in 597.

The Anglican Communion is a communion of 42 autonomous and interdependent churches united by faith, order, and mutual service. The personal and pastoral ministry of the Archbishop of Canterbury in the Communion helps to strengthen these bonds of communion, working collegially with other primates.

content: A Pastoral Ministry of Unity

content.text:
As an Instrument of Communion, the role of the Archbishop of Canterbury is often expressed through the title 'primus inter pares', meaning 'first among equals' alongside the other Primates (the senior archbishops or presiding bishops) of the Communion's member churches.

A fundamental part of this mandate is an ongoing and vital pastoral ministry. The Archbishop makes visits to the provinces of the Anglican Communion to encourage local Anglicans, support their diverse ministries, and understand firsthand the unique challenges and opportunities they face.

This personal presence is also central to the Archbishop's ecumenical role, fostering relationships with other Christian churches worldwide by building deep and authentic relationships with other Christian leaders.

content: Formal responsibilities of the office

content.text: Alongside their ministry in the Church of England, at the international level, the Archbishop of Canterbury serves the Anglican Communion and works with other instruments.

content: The Primates' Meeting: The Archbishop convenes and chairs this more frequent meeting of the leaders of the member churches for prayer, consultation, and spiritual reflection. They do so together with the Standing Committee of the Primates' Meeting, composed of five archbishops representing each region of the Anglican Communion.
The Lambeth Conference: Brings together bishops from across the Communion to attend this consultative meeting, which has historically taken place approximately every ten years.
The Anglican Consultative Council: Invites 2–3 representatives from each member church of the Anglican Communion. This consultative council brings together bishops, clergy, and laity.
Appointment of the Archbishop

content.text:
The process for appointing a new Archbishop of Canterbury is led by the Crown Nominations Commission (CNC). The Anglican Communion Office (ACO) supports the CNC in its relationship with the Communion.

The CNC for the last Archbishop was a body of 20 members that included five representatives from the Anglican Communion, ensuring a global perspective in this vital appointment. These five representatives came from Africa; the Americas; the Middle East and Asia; Oceania; and Europe.

content: For more information, visit the Archbishop of Canterbury's website.
The Rt Revd and Rt Hon Dame Sarah Mullally DBE, Archbishop-designate of Canterbury
The 106th Archbishop of Canterbury

content.text:
The Rt Revd and Rt Hon Dame Sarah Mullally DBE was announced as the 106th Archbishop of Canterbury in October 2025.

Formerly a senior nurse and the youngest Chief Nursing Officer in England, she was ordained in 2002.

Speaking about the Anglican Communion, the Archbishop of Canterbury has said:

"When I think of the Anglican Communion, I am
filled with joy and hope. As a vibrant part of God's
universal church, it serves millions of Christians
around the world, spanning diverse cultures and
traditions. I give thanks for the churches of the
Anglican Communion and their faithful Christian presence
in communities around the world.

Through the deep bonds of friendship shared
among the provinces, I know that every day the
Anglican churches strengthen one another in
mission; stand together in times of
adversity and raise their voice on matters of injustice
and wrong.

This is possible because, as Christians, we are all
called to one hope. Paul's letter to the
Ephesians says: "... We all share one hope, one Lord, one
faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who
is above all and through all and in all."

Watch a video with the full message shared by the Archbishop of Canterbury with the Anglican Communion, on the announcement of her nomination – October 2025.

content: The Primates' Meeting

The Primates' Meeting:
A forum for fellowship and consultation

content.text: As one of the four Instruments of Communion, the Primates' Meeting plays a unique and fundamental role in the life of the Anglican Communion. It brings together the most senior bishops, archbishops, and moderators—known as 'Primates'—of the autonomous member churches of the Anglican Communion and provides a forum for these senior leaders to consult on shared challenges and opportunities.

content: Structure and Meeting

content.text: The Primates' Meeting operates through a distinct structure:

content: The Archbishop of Canterbury: Convenes the meeting as Primus inter pares ("first among equals"). The Archbishop acts as a focus of unity for the Communion, serving as convener, chair, and mediator.

Primates' Standing Committee: This committee, composed of regional primates, plans the meetings and sets the agenda. This role is fundamental to fostering dialogue and seeking to forge consensus on behalf of the Communion.
The role of the Secretary General: The Secretary General of the Anglican Communion supports the Primates' Meetings as part of their responsibilities.

Provincial autonomy: A cornerstone of Anglican polity is that each member church is autonomous. The authority of the Primates' Meeting is one of moral persuasion, not of canonical legislation. Its communiqués are not legally binding on any member church.
Walking together

content.text: Established in 1978 by the 101st Archbishop of Canterbury, Donald Coggan, the original vision of the meeting was primarily pastoral and relational. It was conceived as an intimate forum for the leaders of the rapidly diversifying global family of churches to offer mutual support and discern together God's mission. The meetings are rooted in "prayer, conversation, Bible study, and fellowship", providing a space where spiritual leaders can share their vision.

content:
The history of the Meeting reflects the nature of "relational authority" within a decentralized global body. It has been the principal place where the Communion's leadership has faithfully addressed different perspectives on significant issues.

The Primates' Meeting remains a vital forum for encounter, with the 2024 Primates' Meeting in Rome deliberating on the broad changes considered in the IASCUFO document "The Nairobi-Cairo Proposals", as well as including a shared pilgrimage and a historic encounter with Pope Francis.

The ACO also recognizes that not all primates have attended recent meetings, reflecting the different ways in which provinces are managing disagreements within the Communion.

At the formal Primates' Meetings, the Primates of each region elect a Regional Primate to represent them on the ACC Standing Committee and to serve as the Standing Committee of the Primates' Meeting. In recent years, the Regional Primates have also helped to provide pastoral support in their regions when such help was requested, in coordination with the Anglican Communion Office and the Archbishop of Canterbury.

The Lambeth Conference

content.text:
The Lambeth Conference:
A global gathering of bishops

content:
The Lambeth Conference is one of the four Instruments of Communion that provide cohesion and guidance to the global Anglican family.

It is an international assembly of Anglican bishops, convened by the Archbishop of Canterbury approximately every ten years. Its purpose is to discuss matters of the church and the world and collectively shape the global mission of the Anglican Communion for the next decade.

The 15th Lambeth Conference, held in 2022, was guided by the theme 'God's Church for God's World'.

The conference consisted of three phases:
Phase 1 – Listening together: An online preparatory phase where bishops and spouses gathered to study the Bible, pray, and converse on key themes.
Phase 2 – Walking together: The in-person meeting in Canterbury, which brought together more than 600 bishops and spouses from around 165 countries for worship, study, and deliberation.

Phase 3 – Witnessing together: An ongoing phase (2023–2026) that invited the whole Communion to explore the Lambeth Calls and 'Add your voice to the call'. A series of global webinars and local group discussions were produced to advance the calls.

The main outcomes of the 2022 conference were the Lambeth Calls. These invited the churches to discern and commit to action on 10 key themes, including discipleship, Safe Church, Anglican Identity, and the Environment. The Episcopal Ministry team (EMAC) of the Anglican Communion Office supports bishops and the wider church in carrying these calls forward.

Other key outcomes included:
The Lambeth Calls that related to key themes in the church and in world affairs.
New initiatives: The formal launch of the Anglican Communion Science Commission and the Communion Forest, a new global environmental initiative.

Statements of Support: The bishops also collectively issued 14 "Statements of Support" addressing specific situations of concern around the world.

Read more about the Lambeth Conference on the official website.

content.text: Learn more about the instruments of communion

content: The Lambeth Conference has met since 1867, playing a historic role in shaping Anglican identity. In 1888, the conference confirmed the Chicago-Lambeth Quadrilateral. Explore the other Instruments of Communion that, together with the Lambeth Conference, provide cohesion and guidance to the global Anglican family.
